title: A museum after normal hours
content:
A city museum introduced an evening opening programme to find out whether its normal hours excluded potential visitors. The programme used the existing galleries and did not include a new exhibition. Staff expected the later hours to appeal to some people who could not visit during the day, but they did not assume that every non-visitor faced the same obstacle. Transport, cost, confidence and interest could each influence a decision to attend. The museum treated the programme as a limited trial, with decisions about permanent opening hours deferred until staff had examined both attendance and visitors' experiences.

The museum opened late on one weekday each week throughout the trial. Admission to the collection remained free, although visitors still paid for food and drinks. Two galleries closed earlier than the others because their staffing arrangements could not be extended. Notices at the entrance identified those rooms so that visitors would not discover the restriction only after walking across the building. The museum did not consider a partly open building ideal, but it preferred to state the limit plainly while testing whether the broader change was useful.

To learn who attended, the museum used short exit interviews and an optional online questionnaire. Interviewers approached every fifth departing adult rather than choosing people who looked willing to talk. Some selected visitors declined, and their absence from the responses was recorded. The online form was promoted through the museum's mailing list as well as inside the building. Staff recognised that this route would reach people already interested in the institution more easily than residents with little connection to it. Combining the two sources increased the range of comments but did not turn the responses into a representative sample of the whole city.

Several respondents described fitting a visit around work, but work was not the only reason for coming later. Others preferred the quieter atmosphere or arranged to meet friends after dinner. Some had visited the museum recently during normal hours. The team consequently distinguished an evening visit from a first visit: moving an existing visitor from one time slot to another was a different outcome from reaching someone who had previously stayed away. Attendance totals alone could not separate these effects. Interview questions about earlier visits were included to make the distinction possible.

The comments also revealed different preferences about gallery activity. Some visitors welcomed informal conversations with staff, while others wanted to look without interruption. The museum responded by identifying places where a short conversation could take place and leaving other areas quieter. It did not instruct staff to approach everyone. The change was intended to offer a choice rather than to define a single ideal evening experience. A visitor who remained silent might be deeply engaged with an object, so the number of conversations was not treated as a direct measure of attention.

Operational records were considered alongside visitor feedback. A late closing affected cleaning schedules and the following morning's preparation even when the number of visitors was modest. Staff noted these effects in a shared log rather than estimating them solely from attendance. The trial account describes the adjustments but does not give a total cost for each evening. Nor does it compare the programme with evening openings at other museums. These limits matter when the account is used outside the institution: evidence that a change was manageable in one building is not evidence that it would be equally simple everywhere.

At the end of the trial, managers kept the evening programme on a provisional basis and planned another review. They considered the interviews useful for identifying different reasons for visiting, but did not claim to have established the programme's effect on the whole population. The next stage would seek views from people who had not attended, including people outside the museum's existing contact lists. Understanding why an opportunity goes unused requires more than asking those who have already taken it up.

questions.question: The evening programme coincided with the launch of a new exhibition.
questions.instructions: Do the following statements agree with the information in the passage? Choose TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.
questions.evidence: The programme used the existing galleries and did not include a new exhibition.
questions.explanation: The programme used existing galleries and explicitly did not include a new exhibition.
questions.trap: Do not infer that extended hours were part of an exhibition launch.
questions.tip: Check the whole claim, including qualifiers. FALSE needs contrary evidence; NOT GIVEN needs an information gap.

analysis.keyEvidence: did not include a new exhibition
passageKeywords: did not include a new exhibition

paraphrasePairs.question: launch of a new exhibition
paraphrasePairs.passage: did not include a new exhibition

questions.question: All galleries remained open for the whole evening.
questions.instructions: Do the following statements agree with the information in the passage? Choose TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.
questions.evidence: Two galleries closed earlier than the others because their staffing arrangements could not be extended.
questions.explanation: Two galleries closed early, which directly contradicts all galleries staying open throughout.
questions.trap: All is stronger than most or some.
questions.tip: Check the whole claim, including qualifiers. FALSE needs contrary evidence; NOT GIVEN needs an information gap.
